name: Glass-Steagall Act
kicker: New Deal banking law of 1933 · Created the FDIC and split banking in two
briefing: In the early 1930s, thousands of American banks failed, and families lost their life savings. The Banking Act of 1933, named for Senator Carter Glass and Representative Henry Steagall, created the FDIC to insure bank deposits and built a wall between commercial banks, which hold people’s savings and make loans, and investment banks, which help companies sell stocks and bonds. That wall stood for 66 years, until Congress repealed key parts of it in 1999.
answerHtml: Glass–Steagall Act (or Banking Act of 1933; prompt on Banking Act; do not accept “FDIC,” “Federal Reserve Act,” or “Dodd–Frank”)
reject: dodd frank wall street reform and consumer protection act
second bank of the united states

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Ferdinand Pecora [“peh-KOR-uh”], the chief lawyer for a Senate committee, questioned powerful bankers such as Charles Mitchell of National City Bank about selling risky investments to ordinary customers, building support for this law. Pecora later became one of the first members of the Securities and Exchange Commission.
tossups.r: This law split commercial banks from investment banks. For 10 points, name this 1933 law that also created the FDIC.

tossups.p: Sections 16, 20, 21, and 32 of this law are the parts usually meant by its famous nickname. A 1999 law named for Senator Phil Gramm and Representatives Jim Leach and Thomas Bliley repealed Sections 20 and 32, which had kept banks from owning or sharing leaders with securities firms.
tossups.r: Bill Clinton signed that repeal. For 10 points, name this 1933 law that walled off commercial banking from investment banking.

tossups.p: Two partners at J.P. Morgan and Company, Henry S. Morgan and Harold Stanley, left in 1935 to found Morgan Stanley after this law forced their firm to split its business in two. J.P. Morgan chose to keep taking deposits and making loans.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New Deal law that separated commercial banks from investment banks and created the FDIC.

tossups.p: In 2013, Senators John McCain and Elizabeth Warren proposed bringing back a “21st Century” version of this law. After the 2008 financial crisis, some experts argued that ending parts of this law had helped cause the crisis, while others noted that many of the firms that failed would not have been covered by it.
tossups.r: Congress repealed key parts of it in 1999. For 10 points, name this 1933 law that separated commercial and investment banking.

tossups.p: Twenty years before this law passed, its Senate sponsor helped write the Federal Reserve Act as a congressman from Virginia. That sponsor later served as Woodrow Wilson’s Secretary of the Treasury and then as a senator from 1920 until his death in 1946.
tossups.r: This law’s House sponsor, from Alabama, insisted on federal insurance for bank deposits. For 10 points, name this 1933 law named for both men.

tossups.p: Sanford Weill [“WHILE”] of the Travelers Group and John Reed of Citicorp merged their companies in 1998 to form Citigroup, a deal that was allowed only temporarily under the banking rules of the time, including this law. Travelers owned a large stock brokerage, Salomon Smith Barney.
tossups.r: In 1999, Congress repealed the parts of this law that kept banks and securities firms apart. For 10 points, name this 1933 banking law.

tossups.p: Three months after a national “bank holiday” closed the country’s banks, Congress passed this law near the end of the Hundred Days. The insurance plan it created began protecting accounts on January 1, 1934, covering up to $2,500 per depositor.
tossups.r: That plan was run by a new agency, the FDIC. For 10 points, name this 1933 law that separated commercial and investment banking.

tossups.p: The Federal Reserve’s Regulation Q, which carried out part of this law, banned paying interest on checking accounts and capped the interest banks could pay on savings. Those caps lasted for decades before they were phased out in the 1980s.
tossups.r: This law also created the FDIC to insure deposits. For 10 points, name this 1933 law that separated commercial banking from investment banking.

tossups.p: The Volcker [“VOHL-ker”] Rule, added to the 2010 Dodd–Frank Act, limited how banks could trade investments with their own money, and some commentators compared it to this earlier law. One section of this earlier law that was never repealed still bars securities firms from taking deposits.
tossups.r: Congress repealed other key parts of this law in 1999. For 10 points, name this New Deal banking law that created the FDIC.

tossups.p: Four years after co-sponsoring this law, a congressman from Alabama teamed up with Senator Robert Wagner of New York on a 1937 housing law that created the U.S. Housing Authority. That congressman chaired the House Banking and Currency Committee during the New Deal.
tossups.r: This law also created the FDIC. For 10 points, name this 1933 law named for that congressman and a senator from Virginia.

tossups.p: Federal Reserve chairman Marriner Eccles [“EK-ulz”] pushed for a 1935 banking law that created the Fed’s Board of Governors. That 1935 law also made permanent a temporary plan that this earlier law had set up two years before.
tossups.r: That plan insured bank deposits through the FDIC. For 10 points, name this 1933 law that also separated commercial and investment banking.

tossups.p: The Financial Services Modernization Act, which passed with large majorities of both parties in both houses of Congress, ended key parts of this law. That 1999 act let one company own a bank, a securities firm, and an insurance company together.
tossups.r: President Bill Clinton signed it in November 1999. For 10 points, name this 1933 law that separated commercial and investment banking.

tossups.p: In the 1920s, big banks such as Chase and National City set up “securities affiliates” that sold stocks and bonds, sometimes to the banks’ own depositors. Critics said those affiliates helped fuel the stock market bubble that burst in 1929.
tossups.r: This law forced banks to choose between taking deposits and dealing in securities. For 10 points, name this 1933 law that also created the FDIC.

tossups.p: During the 2008 financial crisis, Congress raised the limit of an insurance program created by this law to $250,000 per depositor, and the Dodd–Frank Act made that limit permanent in 2010. The limit had been $100,000 since 1980.
tossups.r: That program is run by the FDIC. For 10 points, name this 1933 law that separated commercial banking from investment banking.

tossups.p: Starting in the late 1980s, the Federal Reserve let some banks earn a growing share of their income from selling new stocks and bonds through special affiliates, slowly loosening a ban set by this law. Those firms were known as “Section 20 subsidiaries,” after the part of this law that limited them.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1933 law, repealed in part in 1999, that separated commercial and investment banking.

clues.t: A New Deal banking law signed by Franklin Roosevelt in June 1933
Named for its sponsors, Senator Carter Glass of Virginia and Representative Henry Steagall of Alabama
Created the FDIC (Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation) to insure people’s bank deposits
Separated commercial banking (taking deposits and making loans) from investment banking (selling and trading stocks and bonds)
Passed in the Hundred Days, three months after FDR’s national “bank holiday” closed the country’s banks
Thousands of banks failed in the early 1930s; many people blamed banks that had gambled depositors’ money on stocks
The Gramm–Leach–Bliley Act (1999), signed by President Bill Clinton, repealed the parts that kept banks and securities firms apart
The 1998 merger of Citicorp and the Travelers Group into Citigroup pushed Congress to change the rules
Deposit insurance began January 1, 1934, covering up to $2,500 per depositor; the limit reached $250,000 in 2008
Carter Glass had helped write the Federal Reserve Act (1913) and served as Woodrow Wilson’s Treasury Secretary
After the 2008 financial crisis, some blamed the 1999 repeal, while others said many failed firms were never covered by it
The Volcker Rule in the Dodd–Frank Act (2010) limited banks’ trading with their own money; some called it a partial return to the 1933 rules
Ferdinand Pecora’s Senate hearings exposed risky practices at big banks and built support for it; Pecora later joined the first SEC
Charles Mitchell of National City Bank (a forerunner of Citibank) was questioned in the Pecora hearings
Its Sections 16, 20, 21, and 32 built the wall between banks and securities firms; the 1999 repeal removed Sections 20 and 32
Section 21, which was never repealed, still bars securities firms from taking deposits
Regulation Q, based on it, banned interest on checking accounts and capped interest on savings until the 1980s
Morgan Stanley was founded in 1935 when partners left J.P. Morgan and Company, which chose to stay a deposit bank
Henry Steagall, who chaired the House Banking and Currency Committee, insisted on deposit insurance
Steagall also co-sponsored the Wagner–Steagall Housing Act (1937), which created the U.S. Housing Authority
The Banking Act of 1935, pushed by Fed chairman Marriner Eccles, made deposit insurance permanent
In 2013, Senators John McCain and Elizabeth Warren proposed a “21st Century” version to bring it back
The 1999 repeal’s other name was the Financial Services Modernization Act; it let one company own a bank, a securities firm, and an insurer
Sanford Weill of Travelers and John Reed of Citicorp led the 1998 merger that formed Citigroup
From the late 1980s, the Fed let banks earn some income from selling new stocks and bonds through “Section 20 subsidiaries”
In the 1920s, banks such as Chase and National City sold stocks and bonds through “securities affiliates”

trap.title: Law, agency, or Fed?
trap.body: This law created the FDIC, so FDIC clues fill these tossups, but the FDIC is a government agency with its own answer line, and saying “FDIC” when the question asks for “this law” is wrong. Carter Glass also helped write the Federal Reserve Act of 1913, a different law, and the Gramm–Leach–Bliley Act of 1999 and the Dodd–Frank Act of 2010 are later laws that show up in the same questions.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this law” or “this act” plus 1933, the Pecora hearings, or a wall between commercial and investment banks means Glass–Steagall, while “this agency” means the FDIC. Its official name, the Banking Act of 1933, also counts, but plain “Banking Act” earns a prompt because there was also a Banking Act of 1935.
trap.line: Real answer line: Glass–Steagall Act (or Banking Act of 1933; prompt on Banking Act; do not accept “FDIC,” “Federal Reserve Act,” or “Dodd–Frank”)
